chunks: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a house that belonged to a woman, and she had a son and a daughter. The son was absent at sea, and the woman died. Her daughter claimed that her mother had designated this house for her and had sold her shares from it, leaving a portion in the house next to the house of one of our companions. He disliked buying it due to the absence of the son and feared that it might not be permissible for him to buy it, as no news was known of the son. He asked me, 'How long has he been absent?' I said, 'For many years.' He said, 'He waits for his absence for ten years, then he buys.' I said, 'If he waits for her absence for ten years, is it permissible to buy it?' He said, 'Yes.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying property when the owner is missing and no news is known of them?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the ten-year period for a missing person (mafqud) is established as sufficient for heirs to purchase their share of property, thereby resolving the legal uncertainty (gharar) regarding the validity of the transaction. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential approach to balancing the rights of absent heirs with the practical needs of those managing the estate, distinguishing between mere absence and presumed death. The decision underscores the importance of temporal markers in Islamic inheritance law to prevent the stagnation of property ownership.
